6: ## Files:
7:     - simulation_HN_NOE.dat:
8:         contains the backcalculated HN-NOEs for each 1 ns frame in the simulation. Rows = timestep/frame (ns),  columns = atompair in HN-NOE. First column is timestep/frame. Columns are orderede as in experimental file.  
9:     - simulation_methyl_NOE.dat
10:         same as above but for methyl NOE pairs
11:     - simulation_SAXS.dat: 
12:         contains the backcalculated scatter (SAXS) intensity for each 1 ns frame in the simulation. Rows = timestep/frame (ns), columns = q_i 
13:     - BME_simulation_weights.dat
14:         contains the optimized weights for each simulation frame from the BME method. 
15:     - BME_stats_SAXS.dat
16:         SAXS from simulation  after BME reweight
17:     - BME_stats_methyl_NOE.dat
18:          Methyl NOE from simulation  after BME reweight
19:      - hyperparameter_theta.dat
20:         contains calculated chi^2 vs Srel for determination of the hyperparameter theta in the BME method. 
21:     - exp_HN2_NOE.dat
22:         HN NOE experimental file from (2), excluding any intraresidues. 
23:     - exp_methyl_NOE.dat
24:         NOE experimental file from (2), excluding any intraresidues.
25:     - the experimental SAXS file used for reweighting can be found in SAXS_and_SANS directory.

23:                                     Abstract Nanodiscs are membrane mimetics that consist of a protein belt surrounding a lipid
24:                                     bilayer, and are broadly used for characterization of membrane proteins. Here, we investigate the
25:                                     structure, dynamics and biophysical properties of two small nanodiscs, MSP1D1DH5 and DH4H5.
26:                                     We combine our SAXS and SANS experiments with molecular dynamics simulations and previously
27:                                     obtained NMR and EPR data to derive and validate a conformational ensemble that represents the
28:                                     structure and dynamics of the nanodisc. We find that it displays conformational heterogeneity with
29:                                     various elliptical shapes, and with substantial differences in lipid ordering in the centre and rim of
30:                                     the discs. Together, our results reconcile previous apparently conflicting observations about the

430:                                         Analysis of the measured SAXS and SANS revealed an elliptical shape of the DH5-DMPC upon fit-
431:                                     ting of a single structure to the data. In contrast, the structure obtained by fitting the NMR/EPR data

445:                                    axis within the nanodisc and thus give rise to observations of an elliptical shape. By complementing
446:                                    the experiments with MD simulations we obtained a ensemble with structural features that support
447:                                    this hypothesis.
448:                                       We thus quantified the degree of ellipticity in terms of an acylindricity parameter, C, defined as
449:                                    the difference between the x and y components of the gyration tensor (see Materials and methods
450:                                    for details). C is thus a measure of how far from a perfect circular cylinder the shape is, and C = 0
451:                                    corresponds to a circular shape. We calculated both the average and distribution of the acylindricity
452:                                    from the simulated ensemble both before and after reweighting against the experimental data
453:                                    (Figure 3B and C). In addition, we calculated the acylindricity of both the integrative NMR structure
454:                                    and from the structural model obtained from the SAXS and SANS measurements.
455:                                                                                          pﬃﬃﬃ
456:                                       We find that the acylindricity decreased from C ¼ 17 Å in the original MD simulation trajectory
457:                                        pﬃﬃﬃ
458:                                    to C ¼ 15 Å after integration of the NMR and SAXS data, showing that the experiments indeed
459:                                    affect the structural features. This value is in the middle of that obtained from the analytical geomet-
460:                                                                             pﬃﬃﬃ
461:                                    ric model fitted to the SAXS data ( C ¼ 22 Å) and that of the integrative NMR/EPR structure
462:                                     pﬃﬃﬃ
463:                                    ( C ¼ 8 Å) (Bibow et al., 2017). Thus, the acylindricity of the final, heterogenous ensemble lies
464:                                    between that of the two conformations that were fitted as single structures to fit either the NMR or
465:                                    SAXS data.
466:                                       To understand better the elliptical shape of the DH5-DMPC nanodisc and the role played by
467:                                    reweighting against experiments, we calculated the average acylindricity for each cluster of confor-
468:                                    mations of DH5-DMPC both before and after integration with experimental data (Figure 3D). We
469:                                    note that because our reweighting procedure acts on the individual conformations and not at the
470:                                    coarser level of clusters, the average acylindricity changes slightly for each cluster upon reweighting.
471:                                    Clusters 1 and 2, which together constitute about 80% of the conformational ensemble (both before
472:                                    and after reweighting), are both clusters with high acylindricity, but with almost orthogonal direc-
473:                                    tions of the major axis in the elliptical structure. The major change after integration is the exchange
474:                                    in populations of the two clusters resulting in cluster 2 to be weighted highest, underlining the influ-
475:                                    ence and importance of the integration. Thus, our MD simulations and the integration with the
476:                                    experiments support the hypothesis of underlying elliptical fluctuations with the major axis changing
477:                                    direction inside the nanodisc, and we note that the detailed molecular description of this was only
478:                                    possible by combining the MD simulations with both the SAXS and NMR data.
479: 
480:                                    Analyses of the lipid properties in nanodiscs
481:                                    Nanodiscs are often used as models for extended lipid bilayers, but the presence and interactions
482:                                    with the protein belt — and the observed shape fluctuations — could impact the properties of the
483:                                    lipid molecules in the nanodisc compared to a standard bilayer. Building on earlier experimental
484:                                    (Mörs et al., 2013; Martinez et al., 2017) and simulation work (Siuda and Tieleman, 2015;
485:                                    Debnath and Schäfer, 2015) work, we therefore used our experimentally-derived ensemble of
486:                                    nanodisc structures to investigate the properties of lipids in the small DH5-DMPC nanodisc, and
487:                                    compared them to those in a DMPC bilayer. Specifically, we calculated the thickness of the DMPC
488:                                    bilayer (Figure 4A) and the order parameters, SCH , of the DMPC lipids (Figure 4B,C).
489:                                        As done previously (Siuda and Tieleman, 2015; Debnath and Schäfer, 2015), we subdivide the
490:                                    lipid area in the nanodisc into zones dependent on the distance from the MSP protein belts (above
491:                                    or below 10 Å). The results of both the thickness and order parameter analyses show the same
492:                                    trend: a clear difference between the lipids close to the protein belt and those more central in the
493:                                    nanodisc. The results illustrates that the DMPC lipid bilayer in the DH5 nanodiscs is not homoge-
494:                                    neous but rather thinner and un-ordered near the protein belt and thicker and more ordered in the
495:                                    core of the nanodisc, which in turn is more similar to a pure bilayer (Figure 4). These results are in
496:                                    line with previous simulation studies on the larger DMPC nanodiscs, MSP1, MSP1E1 and MSP1E2
497:                                    (Siuda and Tieleman, 2015; Debnath and Schäfer, 2015), albeit performed without experimental
498:                                    reweighting, as well as with solid state NMR data on the both DH5-DMPC and the larger MSP1-
499:                                    DMPC (Mörs et al., 2013; Martinez et al., 2017).

209:                                    and liquid phase, respectively, as they are below and above the melting transition temperature
210:                                    (Martinez et al., 2017) (see also DSC analysis below). We used a standard solution SAXS setup for
211:                                    these measurements, as this at present provides a better control of both the sample temperature
212:                                    and sample concentration than in the SEC-SAXS based measurement. The effect of the DMPC melt-
213:                                    ing transition is clearly reflected in the SAXS data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) where both the
214:                                    position of the first minimum and the shape of the oscillation changes as the DMPC transitions from
215:                                    the gel to the molten state. We observe that the intensity of the forward scattering decreases signifi-
216:                                    cantly with increasing temperature, a result of the small but significant temperature-dependent
217:                                    change of the partial specific molecular volume of the DMPC.
218:                                       To analyze the data, we again applied the molecular constrained geometrical model for the nano-
219:                                    discs (Table 1, Right). Here, the effect of the DMPC melting transition can clearly be seen on the
220:                                    obtained DMPC area per headgroup which increases significantly as a result of the melting. Qualita-
221:                                    tively similar observations of the melting transition of DMPC and DPPC based nanodiscs were previ-
222:                                    ously reported in the MSP1D1 and MSP1E3D1 nanodiscs using DSC, SAXS and fluorescence
223:                                    (Denisov et al., 2005; Graziano et al., 2018). Regarding the shape of the DH5 nanodiscs without
224:                                    the His-tag (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we find parameters similar to those derived from SEC-
225:                                    SAXS/SANS experiments including an elliptical shape with ratios of the two axes between 1.2 and
226:                                    1.4. This observation is in apparent contrast to the recently described integrative NMR/EPR struc-
227:                                    tural model of the DH5-DMPC nanodisc which was found to be more circular (Bibow et al., 2017).
228:                                    We therefore examined the fit to the model varying the axis ratios from 1.0 to 1.6 and indeed find
229:                                    that a number of features are best explained with a slightly asymmetric model (Figure 1—figure
230:                                    supplement 3). Both in the SEC-SAXS/SANS experiments, but perhaps particularly in the standard
231:                                    solution SAXS setup, it is possible that polydispersity in the number of lipids embedded in the nano-
232:                                    discs is present (Skar-Gislinge et al., 2018), and contributes to the shapes obtained from our mod-
233:                                    els (Caponetti et al., 1993). We therefore analyzed our data using a model where we include
234:                                    polydispersity through a normally-distributed number of lipids, parameterized via the relative stan-
235:                                    dard deviation (slip ). Our results show that while a modest level of polydispersity (ca. 1%) cannot be
236:                                    ruled out, greater levels lead to worsening of the fit to the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
237: 
238:                                    Molecular dynamics simulations
239:                                    The results described above suggest an apparent discrepancy of the solution structure of the DH5-
240:                                    DMPC nanodisc when viewed either by NMR/EPR or SAXS/SANS. In particular, the NMR/EPR struc-
241:                                    ture revealed a circular shape whereas the SAXS/SANS experiments suggested an elliptical shape.
242:                                    The two kinds of experiments, however, differ substantially in the aspects of the structure that they
243:                                    are sensitive to. Further, both sets of models were derived in a way to represent the distribution of
244:                                    conformations in the experiments by a single ‘average’ structure.
245:                                       In order to understand the structural discrepancies between the two solution methods better,
246:                                    and to include effects of conformational averaging, we performed atomistic MD simulations of the
247:                                    His-tag truncated DH5-DMPC nanodisc. In these simulations, we mimicked the experimental condi-
248:                                    tions of the standard solution SAXS measurements obtained at 30˚C and used 100 DMPC lipids in
249:                                    the bilayer as found above. We performed two simulations (total simulation time of 1196 ns) using
250:                                    the CHARMM36m force field (Huang et al., 2017). We visualized the conformational ensemble of
251:                                    the DH5-DMPC nanodisc by clustering the simulations, and found that the three most populated
252:                                    clusters represent 95% of the simulations. Notably, these structures all have elliptical shapes, but dif-
253:                                    fer in the directions of the major axis (Figure 2A).
254:                                       We then examined the extent to which the simulations agree with the ensemble-averaged experi-
255:                                    mental data, focusing on the SAXS experiments and NOE-derived distance information from NMR.
256:                                    We calculated the SAXS intensities from the simulation frames using both FOXS (Schneidman-
257:                                    Duhovny et al., 2013; Schneidman-Duhovny et al., 2016, Figure 2B) and CRYSOL (Svergun et al.,
258:                                    1995, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and compared to the corresponding standard solution SAXS
259:                                    experiments obtained at 30˚C. Similarly, we used r 3 -weighted averaging to calculate the effective
260:                                    distances in the simulations and compared them to the previously reported methyl (Figure 2C) and
261:                                    amide NOEs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Bibow et al., 2017). The discrepancy observed
262:                                    between the simulation and the experiments were quantified by calculating c2 (Table 2).

298:                                       The comparison between experiments and simulations reveal an overall good agreement
299:                                    between the two. Interestingly, the simulations agree well with the SAXS data in the q-region where
300:                                    scattering is dominated by the lipid bilayer and where our geometric fitting of the models for SAXS
301:                                    generally are very sensitive. The MD simulation trajectory captures accurately the depth of the SAXS
302:                                    minimum around q = 0.07 Å–1; however, the shoulder observed in the experiments in the range
303:                                    0.15 Å–1–0.20 Å–1 is not captured accurately.
304:                                       Direct comparison of the previously determined integrative NMR/EPR structure (Bibow et al.,
305:                                    2017) to the SAXS data is made difficult by the missing lipids in the structure. We thus built a model
306:                                    of the lipidated structure by first adding DMPC lipids to the NMR/EPR solved structure (PDB ID
307:                                    2N5E), and then equilibrating only the lipids by MD, keeping the protein conformation fixed. When
308:                                    we use this structure to calculate the SAXS data, the back-calculated data overshoots the depth of
309:                                    the SAXS minimum but captures well the shoulder observed in the experimental data (Figure 2B).
310:                                    Thus, neither the MD trajectory nor the NMR/EPR structure fit perfectly with the measured SAXS
311:                                    data.
312:                                       When comparing the simulations to the NMR-derived distances between methyl groups
313:                                    (Figure 2C), we generally find good agreement, but observe a few distances that exceed the experi-
314:                                    mental upper bounds. A similar trend is observed in the comparison to amide NOEs (Figure 2—fig-
315:                                    ure supplement 2) which shows overall good agreement but with a few NOEs violating at similar
316:                                    positions as for the methyl NOEs. As the amide NOEs are mostly sensitive to the local helical struc-
317:                                    ture, the good agreement with this data mostly reflects that the secondary structures are maintained
318:                                    during the simulations.
